A conjecture is given for general grids. ## Theoretical Computer Science Volume 982, 8 January 2024, 114274 # Bipartite instances of INFLUENCE☆,☆☆ https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tcs.2023.114274Get rights and content ## Abstract The game Influence is a scoring combinatorial game that has been introduced in 2021 by Duchêne et al. [5]. It is a good representative of Milnor's universe of scoring games, i.e. games where it is never interesting for a player to miss their turn. New general results are first given for this universe, by transposing the notions of mean and temperature derived from non-scoring combinatorial games. Such results are then applied to Influence to refine the case of unions of segments started by Duchêne et al. [5]. The computational complexity of the score of the game is also solved and proved to be PSPACE-complete. We finally focus on some specific cases of Influence when the graph is bipartite, by giving explicit strategies and bounds on the optimal score on structures like grids, hypercubes or tori. The correlation between Node-Kayles and Bipartite Influence is thus immediate. For the rest of the paper, each instance of Bipartite Influence will be denoted by a bipartite graph $G=(B\cup W,E)$, where B and W correspond respectively to the sets of black and white vertices, and every edge of E is between a vertex of B and W. Moreover, as this paper focuses on scoring games, if there is no possible confusion, the word “game” will refer to a scoring game and not to a classical combinatorial game. The main issue when studying a combinatorial game is the computation of the highest score of each player, by assuming both are playing optimally. This score is well-defined as the game is finite and with no chance nor hidden information. The main results of this paper are described below. In Section 2, we provide the necessary material from scoring combinatorial theory that applies for the game Bipartite Influence. In particular and for the first time, we provide a formal framework inspired from Milnor [10] and Hanner [7], and also from Siegel [12] in combinatorial (non-scoring) game theory for the concept of temperature and mean of a scoring game. In Section 3, we give general basic or known results on Bipartite Influence. In Section 4, we prove that Influence and even Bipartite Influence are PSPACE-complete. The next section deals with Bipartite Influence on graphs having some symmetry properties. As it has been done in several other games, (see Andres et al. [1] and Bensmail et al. [3]), we prove here that symmetries enable the players to ensure a draw. Section 6 is about a refinement of the results of Duchêne et al. [5] on segments, in particular by using the concepts of mean and temperature. Finally, the game is considered on grids with two and three rows, with an exact value or a bound for the score in almost all cases. A conjecture is given for general grids. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- On the rectangle eliminating number of grid graphs - ScienceDirect (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304397526004287) citeturn2search2 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; 10.1016/j.tcs.2026.116199 ... In this paper, we derive exact values for S(n, m) when n ∈ {1, 2, 3} and establish nearly tight bounds for 𝑛=5. For general grids, we refine the Periodic Sampling Construction, ensuring that the error term is linear in the shorter side n and independent of the longer side m. Furthermore, we propose an enhanced Hybrid Construction that extends sub-linear error bounds to a broader class of rectangular grids. Specifically, for the square case with n ≥ 32, we improve the upper bound to 𝑆⁡(𝑛,𝑛)≤2⁢𝑛2/3+4⁢√𝑛+1/3. ## Keywords Rectangle eliminating number ; Grid graph ; Constructive upper bounds ## Introduction The Hitting Set problem is established by Karp as one of the 21 classic NP-complete problems [1]. Over the decades, it has been widely studied in theoretical computer science [2], [3], [4] and has demonstrated significant utility in various practical domains [5], [6]. Formally, given a collection 𝒞 of subsets of a finite set S, a hitting set for 𝒞 is a subset S′⊆S such that S′ contains at least one element from each subset in 𝒞, i.e., for all 𝑇∈𝒞, 𝑆′∩𝑇≠⌀. In this study, we investigate a geometric variant of this problem on grid graphs, originally formulated by Dreyer and Biedl [7]. Pablo Blanco, Robert Dougherty-Bliss, Natalya Ter-Saakov, Doron Zeilberger Jun 05 2026 math.CO arXiv:2606.05439v1 [Button: Scited][Button: Scite!] 0 @misc{2606.05439, author = {Pablo Blanco and Robert Dougherty-Bliss and Natalya Ter-Saakov and Doron Zeilberger}, title = {{I}n {H}ow {M}any {W}ays can a {R}ectangle be {R}ectangled?}, year = {2026}, eprint = {2606.05439}, note = {arXiv:2606.05439v1} }[Button: Copy Citation] PDF There are $2^{n-1}$ ways to tile a $1 \times n$ rectangle with rectangular tiles (of any length, of course they all must have width $1$), but in how many ways can you tile a $100 \times 100$ checkerboard with such tiles? Neither humankind, nor computer-kind, will (most probably) ever know the exact number. But it is possible to compute these numbers for $m \times n$ rectangular grids, if $m$ is not too big, while $n$ can be as big as one wishes. This was initially done in 1988 by David Klarner and Spyros Magliveras, and beautifully extended, around 2006, by, at-the-time, first-year LSU undergraduate Joshua Smith, in collaboration with his faculty mentor, Helena Verrill. Here we extend this to weighted-counting, also keeping track of the number of tiles (that ranges from $1$ to $mn$), and the number of participating grid-edges (that range from $2m+2n$ to $2mn+m+n$). This quickly leads to statistical analyses (mean, variance, and higher moments) of these quantities. While we admire the clever approaches of Klarner-Magliveras and Smith-Verrill, we use two alternative approaches to the original problem, that are more amenable for deriving these generalizations. At the same time, we illustrate the power and beauty of experimental-yet-rigorous enumerative combinatorics. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ChatGPT contributes most proof ideas in a proposed proof of the KLS conjecture · NetGoodIndex (https://netgoodindex.com/events/chatgpt-kls-conjecture-proof-2026) citeturn2search5 [wordlim: 200] Published: last month; Crawled: today; A 4 October 2026 arXiv preprint presents a proof of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture and says most proofs and mathematical ideas were found by ChatGPT; the authors supplied the suspension idea and improved the exposition.
